title: Niall and the Rolling Wagon
markdown:
The Moonfold Mountains were a land of soft rolling hills, a lovely peaceful place to live. Nestled high within them, in a tower that wasn’t too tall, lived a young wizard named Niall. He loved his cozy tower: always warm, always filled with the gentle twinkle of jars holding captured stardust, always dotted with comfy cushions, perfect for quiet thinking. His dearest friend, a very fluffy very white rabbit named Pipkin, was most often found curled on one of these, little nose twitching like a miniature pink flower. Niall was usually a very content wizard, but sometimes, when something new or unexpected happened, his middle felt a little fluttery. He did not like journeys that were too new. Sometimes helping felt like a big unknown step.

One gentle evening, as the moon began to paint silvery stripes, a faint worried sound drifted on the air. Mrs. Willowbrook, his kind neighbour down the winding mossy lane. “Oh, dear, oh dear!” Weary, a bit flustered. “My wagon! It just keeps rolling away, especially on these lovely moonlit nights! If it keeps rolling, I won’t be able to bring my lovely berry pies to the village market tomorrow!”

Niall imagined the wagon wobbling downhill. The fluttery feeling returned. He worried a little about new journeys and about helping, but he knew, deep down, that he should go. “Come along, Pipkin.” Soft, reassuring. Pipkin twitched long white ears, as if to say, I’m right behind you.

They set out, not the usual familiar lane, but a new path through the fern-lit woods. Tall ferns in moonlight shimmered like waves of green lace. A peaceful walk: rustle of leaves, the distant sleepy hoot of an owl. Worry sat like a tiny shy knot. As they ambled, a plump round acorn, nudged by a breeze, tumbled from an old oak, rolled across the path with a soft thud, bounced merrily, and to Niall’s slight dismay rolled off to the side, almost as if pointing the wrong way entirely.

“Oh, no.” A small sigh. His middle did a little flip. “Which way should we go now? Maybe we should go home.”

Pipkin nudged his paw. Silent encouragement. Then a wise old badger, fur a rich warm velvet brown, emerged slowly from a mossy hollow log. “Hullo there, young wizard.” Deep as the earth. “Have you perhaps lost your way? The Willowbrook cottage lies that way,” a kindly claw toward a gentle rise, “just past the old whispering oak.”

Niall offered sincere thanks, calmer with a clear direction, though the rolling acorn had made him wish they were already there.

Soon, Mrs. Willowbrook’s little cottage. Moonlight spilled like warm creamy milk. The wagon sat a little sad, wheels still and silent. Mrs. Willowbrook waited, smile a little wobbly, much like her wagon often was. “Oh, Niall, Pipkin! So very good of you to come. It’s this wheel.” A slightly askew wooden wheel. “It keeps coming loose, and the wagon just rolls away when I’m not holding it tight enough.”

One wheel quite wobbly, a strange angle. They searched and, to their great fortune, found a large wonderfully smooth round stone, perfectly shaped, as if made just for the purpose, to fit snugly and hold the wheel firm.

The stone, though smooth, was quite heavy. Niall knew he would need all his careful wizardly balance and a good dose of gentle strength. A deep steadying breath. He positioned the stone against the wobbly wheel. Concentration, careful leaning and nudging. The wagon gave a tiny almost nervous wobble. For a fleeting moment his middle did that familiar flip-flop, making him want to step away. He held steady. Gently, gently, he pushed until the stone nestled perfectly, holding the wheel firm and still. The wagon stood tall and straight.

Mrs. Willowbrook clapped, a soft happy sound. “Oh, it’s perfect! Just perfect!” Eyes shining. The wagon looked ready for the rolling hills. Warm gentle hugs. “Thank you, my dears. You have made everything so much better.” Quiet contented warmth, nicer and more lasting than any worry. As they waved, the moon seemed to smile, a bright friendly eye in the velvet sky.

Home through the fern-lit woods, moonlight a gentle guiding hand. The path felt familiar and safe. Niall’s middle felt wonderfully settled. He did not flutter, even when a little leaf rustled suddenly; he just kept walking. In the tower the stardust jars twinkled sleepy greetings. Favourite cushion. Pipkin a warm comforting weight. Moonbeams on the floor. Soft sighs. Dreams of moonlit woods and berry pies that would, tomorrow, actually arrive.
